abstract: Existing vision-language models (VLMs) remain unreliable for fine-grained visual perception. In this report, we present WeVisOne-VL (WeChat Vision All-in-One), a powerful VLM that unifies object-level and pixel-level perception through structured next-token prediction. It supports multiple visual tasks including object detection, referring localization, counting, OCR, segmentation, and matting, enabling localization at any user-specific granularity, from points and boxes to masks and alpha mattes. Architecturally, we integrate a lightweight pixel decoder into the VLM via a special <OBJ> token to generate instance-level pixel outputs. We train the model with a three-stage curriculum SFT followed by mixed-task RL. Across over 30 benchmarks, WeVisOne-VL demonstrates leading performance on both object-level and pixel-level tasks, while maintaining robust rejection for object-absent queries. By releasing WeVisOne-VL to the open-source community, we hope to advance VLMs from broad visual understanding toward truly reliable perception systems for real-world deployment.

sections.body: The introduction argues that current VLMs hallucinate non-existent objects, misread unfamiliar descriptions, and miss non-salient instances. The authors present WeVisOne-VL, built on Qwen3-VL at 2B and 4B scales. It casts tasks as next-token prediction over dedicated coordinate tokens and adds a lightweight pixel decoder for dense outputs. Training uses approximately 100M images with fine-grain annotations, in a multi-stage curriculum followed by mixed-task reinforcement learning. The section names a data engine, the model design and the training pipeline. It reports that results are competitive with general-purpose models and specialized vision systems, without giving numbers here.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Current vision-language models are unreliable for fine-grained perception, so this report proposes one model covering object-level and pixel-level tasks.

sections.body: The data engine connects category discovery and referring expressions through a shared knowledge graph built from Wikipedia and WordNet. Candidate boxes come from SAM3 and an in-house open-vocabulary detector, and Qwen3-VL verifies each candidate against its query. Binary masks are generated with SAM2 and keep the query of their box. A matting pipeline combines BiRefNet, MatAnyone2 and a trained annotator to produce alpha labels, with fallbacks and filtering rules stated. Model errors are reviewed after each round, and annotations change only after review confirms a defect. Formal benchmarks are kept out of training and out of feedback-driven construction.
sections.heading: WeVisOne-VL Data Engine
sections.headline: The data engine yields over 100 million images and approximately 3.6 billion bounding-box annotations, with verification and error-driven refinement.

sections.body: The model is Qwen3-VL with two additions: dedicated coordinate tokens with task tags, and a lightweight decoder. For each generated object token, the decoder takes its hidden state, its predicted box, and multi-level features from the vision encoder. A box-guided query decoder follows Deformable DETR, but its queries come from VLM hidden states instead of static embeddings. A dense prediction stage fuses features, predicts a mask with a dynamic kernel, and refines it in three upsampling stages. The whole decoder, including the matting refinement module, contains about 9.6M parameters. Absent targets are written as None.
sections.heading: Model Design
sections.headline: The model writes tasks as text with coordinate tokens and adds a lightweight decoder that turns object tokens into full-resolution masks.

sections.body: Stage 1 adapts the language model on 90M examples for 13K steps with the vision encoder frozen. Stage 2 unfreezes the encoder, raises the input to 1,960 visual tokens and allows up to 500 boxes per response, using about 40M examples for 9K steps. Stage 3 trains the VLM and pixel decoder jointly with a segmentation loss, then fine-tunes the decoder for matting on 130M samples. Reinforcement learning samples G=8 responses per prompt and keeps about 140K uncertainty-selected samples, giving 178K examples in total. The grounding reward uses Hungarian matching and cubed IoU and penalizes missed and duplicate objects.
sections.heading: Training Pipeline
sections.headline: Training uses three supervised fine-tuning stages, then reinforcement learning on uncertainty-selected samples with box-based grounding rewards.

sections.body: Evaluation covers five object-level tasks and two pixel-level tasks, using greedy decoding at temperature 0. Object detection results use F1 averaged over IoU thresholds from 0.5 to 0.95. On COCO, WeVisOne-VL-4B scores 57.1 mean F1 against 54.7 for LocateAnything-3B. On Dense200 it scores 71.3 against 58.7. On referring detection, the table reports rejection rates on absent-target queries alongside F1. The text attributes gains on dense detection to accurate recognition over many small instances. Table 8 covers matting under box prompts, where the model is described as competitive with task-specific models.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: WeVisOne-VL-4B reaches 57.1 mean F1 on COCO and 71.3 on Dense200, above the comparable VLMs listed.

sections.body: The section discusses qualitative comparisons in Figures 5 to 12, covering detection, referring detection, counting, pointing, OCR, segmentation and matting. In counting, the text says Rex-Omni reports 537 rather than 42 on one example, while WeVisOne-VL gives the ground-truth count. In referring detection, the baselines still predict a box when no person matches the query, whereas WeVisOne-VL returns none. In matting, SAM2-Matting makes one apron logo transparent, leaving a hole, while WeVisOne-VL keeps it opaque. Figure 13 shows grounded captions. The examples are selected cases, and the section gives no aggregate statistics.
sections.heading: Qualitative Analysis
sections.headline: Qualitative examples show finer instance separation, correct rejection of absent targets, and cleaner matte boundaries than the baselines.

sections.body: The related work groups prior methods into visual grounding, referring segmentation and instance matting. It cites Kosmos-2, Florence-2, Molmo/PixMo and Rex-Omni for grounded outputs, and LISA, GLaMM and GSVA for referring segmentation. For matting it cites MODNet, Matte Anything and SAM2-Matting, and notes that many evaluations assume a salient foreground or a ground-truth mask prompt. The authors state that they evaluate promptable matting in multi-object scenes using boxes, category names and referring expressions. The section contains no experiments and makes no performance comparison.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work places the model among open-vocabulary detectors, grounded multimodal models, referring segmentation systems and promptable matting methods.

sections.body: The limitations are framed as trade-offs. Limited general-purpose training data may reduce general capability relative to the base model. The model produces structured outputs without chain-of-thought reasoning, which may limit complex reasoning tasks. The approach is limited to single-turn prediction, and integrating an agent framework with multi-turn tool use is proposed as future work. The section also notes that benchmark prompts are clear and unambiguous, while real user instructions are often vague, so intent reasoning is needed for reliability. No quantitative failure analysis is given.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Limitations include possible loss of general capability, no chain-of-thought reasoning, single-turn prediction, and unclear user intent.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes the unified next-token interface, the coordinate tokens, the pixel decoder, the three-stage curriculum and mixed-task reinforcement learning. It states that the model improves mean detection F1 and counting accuracy over comparable-scale VLMs. It also says the model advances text grounding and referring localization, and surpasses the evaluated baselines for referring segmentation and image matting. Qualitative examples are cited for crowded-scene localization and rejection of absent targets. These are summary statements, and the specific figures appear in the earlier results sections.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The model improves detection F1 and counting over comparable VLMs and surpasses the evaluated baselines on referring segmentation and matting.

sections.body: The appendix lists SFT data by task and source across three stages, with sample counts in millions, and the segmentation and matting data sources with sizes. Public matting data is sampled against WDE data at a 1:4 ratio within each batch. The RL set of 178K examples is broken down by task, including 44.0% detection and 4.0% pointing. Hyperparameter tables cover learning rates, steps, batch budgets and distributed training. Pixel decoder warm-up, joint training and matting fine-tuning settings are given, followed by the reward definition for each task.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists training corpus sources and counts, along with hyperparameters, pixel decoder training settings and RL reward definitions.
